v.why: At high learning rates larger batches damp the gradient noise that drives Adam into instability, so increasing batch size helps more there than elsewhere.
Large batches give few updates per epoch, so bigger steps are needed to converge within the fixed budget, making LR increases more beneficial.
With the L2 gradient scaled per minibatch and applied every step, tiny batches apply far more effective shrinkage per epoch, so raising alpha over-regularizes them most.
A single hidden layer has no redundant pathway, so shrinking its weights cuts expressiveness directly, whereas deeper nets can redistribute the function across layers.
Strong L2 applied across more layers multiplicatively shrinks the signal and kills ReLUs, so adding depth hurts more under heavy regularization.
Under standard parameterization, wider layers produce larger pre-activation changes per step, so at high LR extra width pushes training toward divergence.
Narrow nets are capacity-bottlenecked, so the extra compositional expressiveness from another layer helps them more than wide nets that already have ample capacity.
Update-size errors compound multiplicatively across three layers, so deeper nets destabilize sooner as LR rises.
Deeper nets need more optimization steps, which large batches withhold under a fixed epoch budget, so added depth pays off less there.
At tiny learning rates the weights barely move from initialization, so a stronger penalty has little room to shrink them and raising alpha hurts less than at moderate LR.

I kept 10 hypotheses. None of the 20 conditions on the edited field itself, and none switches off the edited component, so the first rule removed nothing. I then dropped duplicates that share a mechanism (step budget, per-batch L2 scaling, width-driven step size) and kept one per field pair. Among the rest I preferred cases where a reasonable expert could bet either way.
